A.explanation: Straight line through origin on $V$ against $I$ gives constant $V/I$, so gradient equals constant resistance of an ohmic metallic conductor.

B.explanation: Curved $V$ against $I$ means $V/I$ changes with $I$, so resistance increases with current due to heating, not ohmic behaviour.

C.explanation: Curved $I$ against $V$ shows non-ohmic behaviour, and gradient is $I/V = 1/R$, not $R$.

D.explanation: Straight $I$ against $V$ is ohmic but gradient is $I/V = 1/R$, so gradient gives conductance, not resistance.

hints: Notice the axes: two graphs plot $V$ on the vertical axis against $I$, and two plot $I$ against $V$ - only one axis choice makes gradient equal $V/I$.
Recall an ohmic metallic conductor at constant temperature has constant resistance with $V = IR$, so $V$ is directly proportional to $I$.
Check which $V$-against-$I$ shape gives a constant $V/I$ gradient through the origin and why the curved shapes imply heating and increasing resistance.
walkthrough: Identify the axes: resistance is $R = V/I$, so for gradient to equal $R$ the vertical axis must be $V$ and the horizontal axis must be $I$.
State the physics: a metallic conductor obeying Ohm's law has constant $R$ at constant temperature, so $V = IR$ is a direct proportion.
Therefore the $V$ against $I$ graph must be a straight line through the origin with constant gradient $\Delta V / \Delta I = R$.
A curved $V$ against $I$ graph means gradient $\Delta V / \Delta I$ increases with $I$ as the wire heats, so it is a non-ohmic filament, not the required constant-resistance line.
Graphs of $I$ against $V$ have gradient $\Delta I / \Delta V = 1/R$, so even the straight-line one gives conductance, not resistance.
Only the straight-line $V$ against $I$ through the origin satisfies both constant resistance and gradient equals resistance. This is option A.
